## How this work is cited

Passages inside Cosmopolitanism: Ethics in a World of Strangers are identified by chapter, or the named strand of the argument. Appiah's book develops two strands — the idea that we have obligations to strangers, and the idea that the value of lives is not measured by proximity. The corpus cites the strands by name on some entries, which is more informative than the chapter alone.

## The work in Kwame Anthony Appiah’s thought

Kwame Anthony Appiah (b. 1954) is a British-Ghanaian philosopher who has taught at Princeton, NYU, and elsewhere. [More on Kwame Anthony Appiah](https://www.philosophydef.com/thinkers/kwame-anthony-appiah) .

4.  > Cosmopolitans begin with a sense of one thing we all certainly share, which is our fallibility. Nobody has reason to be confident that they're right about everything.

5.  > We have obligations to others that stretch beyond those to whom we are related by ties of kith and kind; and we must take seriously the value not just of human life but of particular human lives.

6.  > They know they don't have all the answers. They're humble enough to think that they might learn from strangers; not too humble to think that strangers can't learn from them.
